title: Internal dual and exact Hom of a finite-free retract sheaf
statement:
Let $(C,J,R)$ be a small ringed site with commutative coefficient sheaf and the universe convention [def-weil-size-convention]. In the category of $R$-module sheaves [def-weil-sheaf-of-modules-category], let $T$ have maps $i:T\to R^{\oplus r}$ and $p:R^{\oplus r}\to T$ with $r\geq0$ finite and $pi=1_T$. Write $T^\vee=\mathcal Hom_R(T,R)$ [def-pur-sheaf-hom]. The dual maps give a splitting
$$T^\vee\xrightarrow{p^\vee}(R^{\oplus r})^\vee\xrightarrow{i^\vee}T^\vee,\qquad i^\vee p^\vee=1,$$
and the coordinate-dual identification $(R^{\oplus r})^\vee\cong R^{\oplus r}$ makes this a finite-free retract. For the standard vectors $u_j$ and coordinates $u_j^*$ put $t_j=p(u_j)$ and $\lambda_j=u_j^*i$. On every localized site these satisfy
$$\sum_{j=1}^r t_j\lambda_j=1_T,\qquad \phi=\sum_{j=1}^r\phi(t_j)\lambda_j\quad(\phi\in T^\vee).$$
The canonical sheaf map $\delta_T:T\to(T^\vee)^\vee$, $t\mapsto(\phi\mapsto\phi(t))$, is an isomorphism with inverse $\alpha\mapsto\sum_j\alpha(\lambda_j)t_j$. The functor $\mathcal Hom_R(T,-)$ is naturally a retract of $\mathcal Hom_R(R^{\oplus r},-)\cong(-)^{\oplus r}$ by precomposition with $p$ and $i$, and it sends every short exact sequence of module sheaves to a short exact sequence. All displayed maps and identities commute with restriction to localized sites.

proof.text: Put $P=R^{\oplus r}$. By the sectionwise definition of a module sheaf, the finite product $R^r$ is a sheaf (glue its finitely many coordinates); its coordinate inclusions and projections satisfy $\sum_j u_ju_j^*=1_P$, so it is also the finite coproduct. On $C/U$, a map $R|_U\to F|_U$ is determined by its value $y\in F(U)$ at $1$: on $V\to U$ it sends $a$ to $a\,y|_V$. Thus evaluation on $u_j$ identifies $\mathcal Hom_R(P,F)(U)$ with $F(U)^r$, with inverse $(y_j)\mapsto[(a_j)\mapsto\sum_j a_jy_j]$ on every object over $U$. These formulas are linear, commute with restriction and postcomposition in $F$, and are inverse on every slice. They give a natural sheaf isomorphism $\mathcal Hom_R(P,F)\cong F^{\oplus r}$. For $F=R$ this identifies $P^\vee$ with $P$ by the coordinate duals.

proof.text: Define $p^\vee(\phi)=\phi\circ p$ and $i^\vee(\psi)=\psi\circ i$ on each localized site. Composition and $pi=1_T$ give $i^\vee p^\vee(\phi)=\phi\circ p\circ i=\phi$. Hence these are splitting maps of sheaves. Composing them with the coordinate-dual isomorphism of step 1 displays $T^\vee$ as a retract of $R^{\oplus r}$.

proof.text: For a local section $t$ of $T$, expand $i(t)=\sum_j u_j u_j^*(i(t))$ in $P$ and apply $p$. This gives $t=\sum_jt_j\lambda_j(t)$, where $t_j=p(u_j)$ and $\lambda_j=u_j^*i$. For any section $\phi$ of $T^\vee$ on $C/U$, apply the $R|_U$-linear map $\phi$ to this equality on every $V\to U$: $\phi(t)=\sum_j\phi(t_j)\lambda_j(t)$. Equality on every section of every object of the slice proves the sheaf-map identity $\phi=\sum_j\phi(t_j)\lambda_j$.

proof.text: Evaluation defines an $R$-linear sheaf map $\delta_T(t)(\phi)=\phi(t)$. Define $\beta(\alpha)=\sum_j\alpha(\lambda_j)t_j$ on every slice; the formula is linear and commutes with restriction. Step 3 gives $\beta\delta_T(t)=\sum_j\lambda_j(t)t_j=t$. Conversely, for every local $\phi$, commutativity of $R$ and linearity of $\alpha$ give $\delta_T\beta(\alpha)(\phi)=\sum_j\alpha(\lambda_j)\phi(t_j)=\alpha(\sum_j\phi(t_j)\lambda_j)=\alpha(\phi)$. Thus both composites are identities, and $\delta_T$ is an isomorphism with precisely the stated inverse.

proof.text: Write $G(F)=\mathcal Hom_R(T,F)$ and $H(F)=\mathcal Hom_R(P,F)$. Precomposition gives $s_F:G(F)\to H(F)$, $f\mapsto fp$, and $q_F:H(F)\to G(F)$, $h\mapsto hi$, with $q_Fs_F=1$. For a map $v:F\to F'$, associativity gives $H(v)s_F=s_{F'}G(v)$ and $G(v)q_F=q_{F'}H(v)$. Hence $s,q$ are natural splitting transformations. In the next steps composition is written right to left; step 1 identifies $H(v)$ with the coordinate map $v^{\oplus r}$.

proof.text: Take a short exact sequence $0\to A\xrightarrow{a}B\xrightarrow{b}D\to0$ in the abelian category of module sheaves. The sequence of $r$th powers is short exact by the following universal-property calculation. For $k:Z\to B^r$ killed by $b^r$, each coordinate $\pi_jk$ factors uniquely through the kernel $a$; the tuple of these factors is the unique factor of $k$ through $a^r$, and $a^r$ is monic by coordinates. If $z:D^r\to Z$ satisfies $zb^r=0$, then $z\iota_jb=0$ for each coordinate inclusion $\iota_j:D\to D^r$; since $b$ is epic, $z\iota_j=0$, and therefore $z=\sum_j z\iota_j\pi_j=0$. The same argument applied to the difference of two maps proves that $b^r$ is epic. Thus $H(a)$ is a kernel of $H(b)$ and $H(b)$ is epic, using step 1. This uses categorical epimorphisms, not surjectivity of sections.

proof.text: First $G(a)$ is monic: if $G(a)u=0$, naturality gives $H(a)s_Au=s_BG(a)u=0$, so $s_Au=0$ by step 6 and $u=q_As_Au=0$; apply this to differences to obtain monicity. Also $G(b)G(a)=0$. For $k:Z\to G(B)$ with $G(b)k=0$, we have $H(b)s_Bk=0$. The kernel property from step 6 gives a unique $h:Z\to H(A)$ with $H(a)h=s_Bk$. Then $G(a)q_Ah=q_BH(a)h=q_Bs_Bk=k$. Its factor through $G(a)$ is unique by monicity. This proves that $G(a)$ is a kernel of $G(b)$.

proof.text: If $z:G(D)\to Z$ satisfies $zG(b)=0$, naturality implies $(zq_D)H(b)=zG(b)q_B=0$. Since $H(b)$ is epic by step 6, $zq_D=0$, hence $z=zq_Ds_D=0$. Subtracting two maps proves that $G(b)$ is epic. Together with step 7 this is the required short exactness of $0\to G(A)\to G(B)\to G(D)\to0$.

proof.text: Finally, localization is sectionwise restriction and successive localization is relocalization. All formulas above use only the restrictions of $i,p$, the standard coordinate inclusions and projections, finite sums, scalar multiplication, evaluation and composition. For an arrow $V\to U$, each such operation is unchanged by passing from $C/U$ to $C/V$; for example $(\sum_j\alpha(\lambda_j)t_j)|_V=\sum_j(\alpha|_V)(\lambda_j|_V)(t_j|_V)$. The internal-Hom restriction is the restriction of slice maps, so this checks the displayed maps and identities on every localized site. If $r=0$, $pi=1_T$ forces $T=0$ and all formulas are empty sums; the arguments also hold for the zero ring and empty covering objects.
